lines.text: - **Limit:** this set is bounded by the hardening vocabulary. "The hand of the Lord" texts that use **no** hardening or heaviness word are **not in it**. Examples: "the hand of the Lord has gone out against me" (Rut 1:13); "your hand has come down on me" (Psa 38:2). See §4.

answer.reason: the limit of the set read and the fuller pass proposed

lines.text: | **"Heavy / hard" hand, chains, sword, breath** (*kaved*, *qashah*, *qasheh*) | 1Sa 5:6, 5:7, 5:11; Psa 32:4; Lam 3:7; Isa 27:1, 27:8; Isa 30:27 ("thick" smoke); Jer 20:7 ("stronger"); Mat 25:24 ("a hard man"); Mal 3:13 ("hard words") | humans under it, or the narrator describing them. **In this set, God never calls his own hand heavy or hard** | as **experience**: terror, affliction, wasting, being walled in, fear |

| **"Strong / mighty hand and outstretched arm"** (*chazaq*) | the Exodus formula: Exo 6:1; 13:9; Deu 3:24; 4:34; 5:15; 6:21; 7:8; 7:19; 9:26; 11:2; 26:8; Jos 4:24; 1Ki 8:42; 2Ch 6:32; Neh 1:10; Psa 89:13; 136:12; Isa 40:10; Jer 21:5; 32:21; 50:34; Eze 20:33–34; Dan 9:15; Exo 32:11; Pro 23:11 | God, Moses, the creed, prayers | as **deliverance remembered**, taught to children (Deu 6:21), and pleaded in prayer (Deu 9:26; Dan 9:15) |

- The Philistines under the ark: "his hand is **hard** against us and against Dagon our god" (1Sa 5:7). The narrator states the experience ("heavy … he terrified and afflicted them", 5:6; "a deathly panic … very heavy", 5:11), and the Philistines read it as intent to kill: "to kill us and our people" (5:10).

- The psalmist: "day and night your hand was **heavy** upon me; my strength was dried up" (Psa 32:4). **The context gives the cause, and it is inside the psalmist:** "**when I kept silent**, my bones wasted away" (32:3). **The heaviness ends at confession:** "I acknowledged my sin … and you forgave" (32:5). The psalm opens with the outcome God intended: "Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven" (32:1).

- **Lam 3.** "He has made my chains **heavy** … he shuts out my prayer … He is a bear lying in wait for me" (3:7–10). **The same poem then says:** "the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; **for he does not afflict from his heart**" (3:31–33).

- **Mat 25:24–26.** "Master, I knew you to be a **hard** man". The servant names the source of his perception himself: "**so I was afraid**, and I went and hid your talent" (25:25). The master answers "You wicked and slothful servant!" (25:26). **The perception of hardness is born of fear, and the parable condemns it.**

- **Isa 59:1–2.** "the Lord's hand is **not shortened**, that it cannot save, or his ear **dull** [*kaved*]". The felt absence of God's hand has a stated cause: "**your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God**, and your sins have hidden his face from you". **What is felt as God's weakness or deafness is the human separation.**

- **Mal 3:13–15.** "Your words have been **hard** against me". The hard words are the human verdict on God: "It is vain to serve God … Evildoers … prosper". **The hardness is in the human perception of God's ways**, and 3:16 answers with those who feared the Lord and "a book of remembrance".

3. **The one who is overpowered for good perceives God as stronger, not as hard.** "O Lord, you have deceived me … **you are stronger than I**, and you have prevailed" (Jer 20:7). The force is **the word**: "a burning fire shut up in my bones" (20:9). **The perception is of a strength he cannot resist, not of cruelty.** Compare M02 §15, the prophet as vessel.

4. **The same hand is "hard" or "saving" depending on which side one stands.** Toward Egypt it is "great deeds of terror" (Deu 4:34; 26:8; Jer 32:21). Toward Israel it is "brought us out" (Deu 6:21). In Jer 21:5, **Israel finds itself on Egypt's side of the formula**: "I myself will fight against you with **outstretched hand and strong arm**, in anger and in fury". **The hand does not change; the person's position before it changes.**

| **Righteousness and justice**, with steadfast love and faithfulness | "You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand … **Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you**" (Psa 89:13–14). "The Lord our God is **righteous in all the works that he has done**" (Dan 9:14), then "who brought your people out … with a mighty hand" (9:15), then "according to all your righteous acts, let your anger … turn away" (9:16) |

| **Love and the sworn oath** | "it is **because the Lord loves you and is keeping the oath** … that the Lord has brought you out with a mighty hand" (Deu 7:8). The same passage goes on: "repays to their face those who hate him" (7:10) |

| **Steadfast love** (*chesed*) | "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, **for his steadfast love endures forever**" (Psa 136:12). The refrain covers the striking of the firstborn (136:10) and the overthrow of Pharaoh (136:15). "He does not retain his anger forever, **because he delights in steadfast love**" (Mic 7:18) |
| **Advocacy for the weak** | "their **Redeemer is strong**; he will plead their cause" (the fatherless, Pro 23:11; the oppressed, Jer 50:34) |
| **Discipline** | "consider the **discipline** of the Lord your God, his greatness, his mighty hand" (Deu 11:2); "that he might discipline you" (Deu 4:36) |

| **Covenant purpose, through judgment** | "with a mighty hand … and with wrath poured out **I will be king over you** … I will enter into judgment with you … **and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant**" (Eze 20:33–37) |
| **Removal of sin** | after "his fierce breath", "**by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for**" (Isa 27:8–9) |
| **The shepherd's arm** | "his **arm** rules for him … He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs **in his arms**" (Isa 40:10–11). **The same arm rules and carries** |

| **Anger** (named, and set inside a purpose) | Jer 21:5 ("in anger and in fury"); Isa 30:27 ("burning with his anger"). The purpose that follows: "the way of life and the way of death" (Jer 21:8); "when the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26) |
| **Holiness against idols** [Claude reading: inferred, not stated] | 1Sa 5: the heavy hand comes when the ark is set beside Dagon, and Dagon falls (5:3–4). No sin of Ashdod's people is named |

- **The heaviness has its source in God's character**, and the texts name **righteousness and justice** (Psa 89:14; Dan 9:14, 16) **together with** steadfast love, faithfulness, the oath, and the cause of the weak.
- **Nowhere in this set is the source a hardness in God.** Lam 3:33 states outright that it is not **from his heart**.

The set here was bounded by hardening and heaviness words. **The fuller answer is in the "hand of the Lord / your hand against / upon me" texts**, which use no such word. Examples: Rut 1:13 ("the hand of the Lord has gone out against me"); Job 19:21 ("the hand of God has touched me"); Psa 38:2; 39:10; 1Sa 7:13; Eze 1:3 and 3:14 (the hand on the prophet).

lines.text: - **M02 unit 2** (divine anger as borne by the human) is directly served by §2: Psa 32:3–5; Lam 3:7, 31–33; Isa 59:1–2. These are human bearings of God's action. Pointer only.

- **Candidate synthesis theme**, a candidate only: "**the heavy hand is how the hidden, fearful or opposed human experiences the strong hand**; the texts separate God's action from his heart (Lam 3:33)."

findings.text: The heavy or hard hand, chains, sword and breath (kaved, qashah, qasheh: 1Sa 5:6, 5:7, 5:11; Psa 32:4; Lam 3:7; Isa 27:1, 27:8; Isa 30:27; Jer 20:7; Mat 25:24; Mal 3:13) is spoken of by humans under it, or by the narrator describing them; in this set God never calls his own hand heavy or hard; it is framed as experience: terror, affliction, wasting, being walled in, fear.

The "strong / mighty hand and outstretched arm" (chazaq) is the Exodus formula (Exo 6:1; 13:9; Deu 3:24; 4:34; 5:15; 6:21; 7:8; 7:19; 9:26; 11:2; 26:8; Jos 4:24; 1Ki 8:42; 2Ch 6:32; Neh 1:10; Psa 89:13; 136:12; Isa 40:10; Jer 21:5; 32:21; 50:34; Eze 20:33-34; Dan 9:15; Exo 32:11; Pro 23:11), spoken by God, Moses, the creed and prayers; it is framed as deliverance remembered, taught to children (Deu 6:21), and pleaded in prayer (Deu 9:26; Dan 9:15).

The Philistines under the ark: "his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god" (1Sa 5:7); the narrator states the experience ("heavy ... he terrified and afflicted them", 5:6; "a deathly panic ... very heavy", 5:11), and the Philistines read it as intent to kill: "to kill us and our people" (5:10).

The psalmist: "day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up" (Psa 32:4); the context gives the cause inside the psalmist, "when I kept silent, my bones wasted away" (32:3); the heaviness ends at confession, "I acknowledged my sin ... and you forgave" (32:5); the psalm opens with the outcome God intended: "Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven" (32:1).

Lam 3: "He has made my chains heavy ... he shuts out my prayer ... He is a bear lying in wait for me" (3:7-10); the same poem then says "the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart" (3:31-33): the chains are felt as heavy, and the poet confesses that the affliction does not come from God's heart; here the action and the heart are explicitly not the same.

Mat 25:24-26: "Master, I knew you to be a hard man"; the servant names the source of his perception himself, "so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent" (25:25); the master answers "You wicked and slothful servant!" (25:26): the perception of hardness is born of fear, and the parable condemns it.

Isa 59:1-2: "the Lord's hand is not shortened, that it cannot save, or his ear dull [kaved]"; the felt absence of God's hand has a stated cause, "your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you": what is felt as God's weakness or deafness is the human separation.

Mal 3:13-15: "Your words have been hard against me"; the hard words are the human verdict on God, "It is vain to serve God ... Evildoers ... prosper"; the hardness is in the human perception of God's ways, and 3:16 answers with those who feared the Lord and "a book of remembrance".

The one who is overpowered for good perceives God as stronger, not as hard: "O Lord, you have deceived me ... you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed" (Jer 20:7); the force is the word, "a burning fire shut up in my bones" (20:9); the perception is of a strength he cannot resist, not of cruelty.

The same hand is "hard" or "saving" depending on which side one stands: toward Egypt it is "great deeds of terror" (Deu 4:34; 26:8; Jer 32:21), toward Israel it is "brought us out" (Deu 6:21), and in Jer 21:5 Israel finds itself on Egypt's side of the formula, "I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury"; the hand does not change, the person's position before it changes.

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Righteousness and justice, with steadfast love and faithfulness: "You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand … Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you" (Psa 89:13–14). "The Lord our God is righteous in all the works that he has done" (Dan 9:14), then "who brought your people out … with a mighty hand" (9:15), then "according to all your righteous acts, let your anger … turn away" (9:16)

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Love and the sworn oath: "it is because the Lord loves you and is keeping the oath … that the Lord has brought you out with a mighty hand" (Deu 7:8). The same passage goes on: "repays to their face those who hate him" (7:10)

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Steadfast love (chesed): "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, for his steadfast love endures forever" (Psa 136:12). The refrain covers the striking of the firstborn (136:10) and the overthrow of Pharaoh (136:15). "He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love" (Mic 7:18)
The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Advocacy for the weak: "their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause" (the fatherless, Pro 23:11; the oppressed, Jer 50:34)
The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Discipline: "consider the discipline of the Lord your God, his greatness, his mighty hand" (Deu 11:2); "that he might discipline you" (Deu 4:36)

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Covenant purpose, through judgment: "with a mighty hand … and with wrath poured out I will be king over you … I will enter into judgment with you … and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant" (Eze 20:33–37)
The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Removal of sin: after "his fierce breath", "by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for" (Isa 27:8–9)

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, The shepherd's arm: "his arm rules for him … He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms" (Isa 40:10–11). The same arm rules and carries

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Anger (named, and set inside a purpose): Jer 21:5 ("in anger and in fury"); Isa 30:27 ("burning with his anger"). The purpose that follows: "the way of life and the way of death" (Jer 21:8); "when the Lord binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow" (Isa 30:26)

The context names as the source of the heavy hand, Holiness against idols [Claude reading: inferred, not stated]: 1Sa 5: the heavy hand comes when the ark is set beside Dagon, and Dagon falls (5:3–4). No sin of Ashdod's people is named

The heaviness has its source in God's character: the texts name righteousness and justice (Psa 89:14; Dan 9:14, 16) together with steadfast love, faithfulness, the oath, and the cause of the weak; anger is named too, but never as the last word, standing inside a purpose of covenant, atonement and healing.
Nowhere in this set is the source a hardness in God: Lam 3:33 states outright that the affliction is not from his heart.
Hardness is felt, and named, by those under the hand; God calls his own hand strong.
The heavy hand is how the hidden, fearful or opposed human experiences the strong hand; the texts separate God's action from his heart (Lam 3:33).
